title: k says /k/
parentNote: Today's letter makes a sound your child already owns: k says /k/, exactly the same back-of-the-tongue pop that c made a few days ago. Two letters, one sound — and that is the whole lesson, so say it plainly rather than letting them think k is something new. English does share the job out by a rule, and at this point in the course the rule is beautifully tidy: with an a after it you write c (cat, can, cap), with an i after it you write k (kid, kit, kim). Every word today obeys that, so if they ask why, you have a real answer. The thing that goes wrong is a puffy "kuh" — "kid" becomes "kuh-id" — so clip it short and quiet, and keep a hand on the throat to check it does not buzz into /g/. Tomorrow a third spelling of this same sound turns up, so today is worth getting clean.

activities.mouthCue: The back of your tongue humps up, touches the roof right at the back, and pops. No buzz, no puff of uh after it.
activities.prompt: You have met this sound before — c made it. This is its other letter, and it sounds exactly the same.
Both happen at the back of your mouth. Hand on your throat: one buzzes and one does not.
Three quick pops. Two are made at the back and one is right behind your teeth.
Pop at the back, small vowel, tap at the front.
Nearly kid. The last sound has lost its buzz.
A name this time. It ends with lips shut and humming.
A hiss and a pop, squashed together at the front. Say them both: /s/, /k/.
The longest word yet — six sounds. Read the first half, nap, then the second half, kin, then push them together.
This one says /k/ too — but look which letter is doing it. There is an a next, so it is c's turn.
All three start with the same pop. Everything hangs on the last sound.
One of these has a pop hiding after the hiss.
Stop at the end for one and hum at the end for the other.

activities.text: kim did pat a fat cat.
activities.prompt: Two /k/ sounds in this line, spelled two different ways. Can you spot them?

activities.text: a napkin can fit in a cap.
activities.prompt: Take napkin in two bits: nap, then kin.

activities.text: sam can skip and kim can win.
activities.prompt: Two people doing two things. Read to the word and, then stop for a breath.
